items.title: Do the three quantum forces all unify together?
items.summary: Here in our Universe, there are a series of fundamental forces that all appear to operate independently of one another. There’s gravity, which is an attractive force between all objects with mass and/or energy, governed by Einstein’s general relativity and the curvature of spacetime. There’s electromagnetism, where any particle with an electric charge or an electric or magnetic field is affected by other charges and electromagnetic fields in the environment. There’s the weak nuclear force, which enables particles to change species and to decay from a heavier species into a lighter one. And there’s the strong nuclear force, which holds atomic nuclei together and binds quarks (and antiquarks) together into hadrons. We aren’t sure whether gravity is an inherently quantum force or not, but the other three forces — electromagnetism , the weak nuclear force , and the strong nuclear force — all have quantum field theories that describe them. Although it took decades to ultimately make sense of these three forces, we now know that at least two of them are interrelated: the electromagnetic and weak nuclear force. These are not two completely independent forces, but rather are two “broken” manifestations of a more fundamental, unified force that exists under high-energy conditions: the electroweak force. It makes sense to wonder whether, at still higher energies, the strong nuclear force doesn’t unify with the electroweak force as well: the big idea of grand unification , or of grand unified theories as they’re sometimes known. We don’t know the answer to whether nature ultimately unifies or not, and if so, under what conditions, at which energy scale, or under what framework. But it’s a fascinating idea that continues to generate theoretical interest, and continues to drive the search for experimental signatures. Here’s what we’re seeking. The idea of unification holds that all three of the Standard Model forces, and perhaps even gravity at higher energies, are unified together in a single framework. This idea, although it remains popular and mathematically compelling, does not have any direct evidence in support of its relevance to reality. Only electroweak unification, among all the unified possibilities, has been established. Credit: ABCC Australia, 2015 If you’ve ever seen the Standard Model of elementary particles, you could easily be forgiven for thinking that: the photon governs the electromagnetic force, which works exclusively on particles with an electric charge, the W-and-Z bosons govern the weak nuclear force, and work exclusively on particles with some form of weak charge, and that the gluons govern the strong nuclear force, and work exclusively on particles with some sort of color charge: the quarks, antiquarks, and other gluons. This oversimplified picture is one that we often paint, and it’s mostly true. For most applications, it’s a close enough approximation to being true — a good enough model — that we simply run with it and don’t worry about the tiny caveats where we need to be a little more subtle. But in fundamental physics, those subtle details are often where the next vital breakthroughs are hiding. For the weak interaction, there isn’t just “some form of weak charge,” but a more complicated structure. In the Standard Model, quarks experience all three of these interactions, the charged leptons experience only the electromagnetic and weak interactions, and the uncharged leptons (neutrinos) experience only the weak interactions at all. Looking into this further led scientists to uncover a surprising phenomenon: electroweak unification, the first successful unification of forces in our understanding of physics since Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism. This diagram of the Standard Model particles shows the fermions in the top row, the gauge bosons in the middle row, and the Higgs on the bottom. The lines indicate couplings, and you can see which fermionic particles couple to which of the forces by the blue lines. Everything with mass couples to the Higgs; the only particles which are massless (and hence, do not) are the photon and the gluons. The theoretical graviton, not shown here, couples to everything with energy: all particles and antiparticles. If there are new particles out there, their couplings may reveal their presence, indirectly, through precision measurements that compare the particles’ observed properties with those predicted by the Standard Model. Credit : TriTertButoxy/Stannered at English Wikipedia The key idea came in the early 1960s. In the strong interactions, there was an idea that had been around for a while known as isospin : where there’s a flavor symmetry related to what we now think of as the “up-ness” or “down-ness” of a particle. For example, a proton, having two up and one down quark, has a more “up” isospin than its counterpart, the neutron, with one up and two down quarks, which instead has a more “down” isospin. The equivalent of that idea for the weak interactions is known as weak isospin , where the (left-chiral) particles with positive electric charge have positive weak isospin (positrons, up quarks, down antiquarks, etc.), and the ones with negative electric charge have negative weak isospin (electrons, up antiquarks, down quarks, etc.). The neutrinos, which are uncharged, since they’re all left-handed (left-chiral fermions), have positive weak isospin, and the antineutrinos, which are also uncharged, have negative weak isospin. Weak isospin used to be thought of as the equivalent of “weak charge,” but something was missing. The original idea was that there were only the W-bosons mediating the weak interactions, and that all of the particles were left-chiral only. However, this would lead to a scenario where particles were massless and the symmetry known as CP , where replacing particles with the mirror-image versions of their antiparticles, would be exact. This instead led to a more complex version of the theory, where: there was a neutral Z-boson in addition to the electrically charged W-bosons, the charged fermions that we observed — the quarks and the charged leptons — were superpositions of both left-chiral and right-chiral particles (allowing particles to have mass), and that in addition to “weak charge” or weak isospin, which itself is not conserved, there’s another quantum number that relates electric charge to weak isospin known as weak hypercharge (which is also not conserved), and only a specific combination of weak isospin and weak hypercharge is conserved. The pattern of weak isospin, T3, and weak hypercharge, Y_W, and color charge of all known elementary particles, rotated by the weak mixing angle to show electric charge, Q, roughly along the vertical. The neutral Higgs field (gray square) breaks the electroweak symmetry and interacts with other particles to give them mass. This diagram shows the structure of particles, but is rooted in both mathematics and physics. Credit : Cjean42/Wikimedia Commons Because there’s an intimate relation between weak isospin, weak hypercharge, and electric charge — and also between the W-and-Z bosons and the photon, which arises as part of the same mechanism that leads to the Higgs boson — we learned that the electromagnetic force and the weak force are not two separate, unrelated forces, but rather are part of a single, unified “electroweak” force. items.title: You have more control over reality than you think
items.summary: Is a “red” rose really red? According to Lisa Feldman Barrett, PhD, a University Distinguished Professor of Psychology at Northeastern University, it’s not that simple. While the flower may appear obviously red, the color isn’t an inherent property of the flower itself. Instead, it’s relational, meaning it emerges from the relationship between light, receptors in the eye, and signals processed in the brain. So, if something as basic as color depends on the relationship between the world and the person perceiving it, what about the rest of reality? This thought exercise reveals how each of us contributes to our reality, Barrett says, and how we have more control — more responsibility — than we might think. Seeing the same world differently Barrett uses animals to break down the concept. Humans typically have three types of color receptors, or cones, in the retina, while dogs have only two. Because of this, we may see a rose as red while a dog sees it as muddy brown. We might assume the dog simply can’t see the rose’s “true” red color. We similarly describe humans who may be missing a type of cone and see color differently as “colorblind.” But what if humans typically had four types of cones instead of three? Would the rose objectively be another color, making those of us with three types of cones colorblind? Barrett says even the most basic aspects of what we take to be objective reality are rooted in the relationship between what is out in the world and what is inside us. Together, they create patterns we experience as reality. Even emotional expression is relational The same idea also applies to emotions, such as anger, that we often believe to be objective. Barrett says the so-called universal expressions of emotion are really stereotypes. For example, if you know nothing about a person, you may interpret a scowl as a sign of anger. But that meaning isn’t inherent in the signal itself. People in Western culture scowl only about 35 percent of the time when they’re angry, according to Barrett. So, if you assume a scowl is the universal expression of anger, you would miss 65 percent of the cases in which someone is angry. “Part of what you did when you were a young child is that you learned patterns for anger, sadness, happiness, and fear,” she says. “If you cried or you observed somebody else crying and that experience was labeled as anger, then you would learn that as an instance of anger. And then that experience would become part of your remembered past — part of your Perception Box” — the invisible mental frame through which each of us experiences the world. Understanding that every experience is shaped by a combination of the remembered past and the sensory present gives you more control over your actions and experiences than you may have thought, Barrett points out. However, that control doesn’t necessarily look the way you’d expect. Expanding the realities you can access For example, if you’re hungry and can choose between potato chips and an apple, the conventional idea of self-control is that you inhibit your desire for the potato chips and choose the apple instead. But the idea of relational realism suggests there are other forms of control available to us. Say you begin eating many types of apples, learning about them, and maybe become an apple expert. As a result, your remembered past changes, and you may become more likely to choose the apple over the potato chips. “Ultimately, this means you have more control over the aspects or features of reality that are available to you in a given moment and which ones are not,” Barrett says. “That control also implies more responsibility when we consider other humans.” Our influence also extends beyond our own reality. The way we behave toward others can, in some ways, influence their actions, Barrett says. “That is the notion of karma,” she says. “And karma is a really good simplification for the idea that you are partly in control and therefore partly responsible for the world that you have to cope with.” We interviewed Lisa Feldman Barrett for Relational Realism , a Big Think interview series created in partnership with Unlikely Collaborators . As a creative non-profit organization, they’re on a mission to help people challenge their perceptions and expand their thinking. Often that growth can start with just a single unlikely question that makes you rethink your convictions and adjust your vantage point. Watch the second episode above, and visit Perception Box to see more in this series. This video You have more control over reality than you think is featured on Big Think .

items.title: I Will Never Be the Pianist My Father Loves Best
items.summary: An excerpt from Hudson by Hernán Ronsino, translated by Mallory Craig-Kuhn When Navia finally says my father is dead, I am about to go on stage to play. I don’t know why it is that in transcendent moments I always think of trivial things: the world opens out into a multitude of dots, and I can’t help but illuminate the lesser plotlines, the hidden sounds. For example: backstage, with my body overtaken by an airy calm, and as I probe the gentle movement of a molar with the tip of my tongue, I think that this city has a river that cuts it in half; a Gothic cathedral; a statue of Leo Tolstoy with one arm longer than the other; and a name that’s impossible to remember. It’s a city in Eastern Europe. Navia’s voice repeats that it just happened. If you want, Juan, we can cancel, he says, we can cancel everything. And he gives my shoulder an exaggerated squeeze; a squeeze that lasts and lingers, that makes me intensely aware of one part of my body. But I want to carry on even though I’m far away, or perhaps precisely because I’m far away. I want to sit at the piano and play while I think about the figure of Tolstoy next to the gentle river. To hear the restless, living movement of the forty people in the audience. I want to carry on. To run with my fingers so the keys become the precise point of pain, the discharge point. And as I play, the word “fugue” and that scene my father described over and over—Bill Turner lost for months in the countryside—appear like a possible harbour, like a light suspended in the dark. After that night, there are three more concerts scheduled in cities very far away. Navia manages to cancel two and move my flight up to the afternoon following my last performance in a city on the shores of the North Sea. Ostende. The truth is, when I find out that’s what the city is called, just like the resort town on the Argentine coast, I tell Navia that he mustn’t call it off, that it has to be the end of the tour. Navia hesitates because it’s the easiest city to cancel and the most expensive to get to. And barely any tickets have sold. I insist. It might sound fickle, but it’ll be the last one, I tell him. There’s a hint of sorrow in my voice, and Navia, who argues with me about everything, bites his tongue and tries to be considerate with me. I think deep down, Navia doesn’t understand why I want to carry on instead of making it back in time for my father’s funeral. It’s raining in Ostende. The signs say: Öostende . A small city, nearly deserted in autumn, that unfolds like a fan against the bay. All the vertical streets descend towards the sea. Or they begin at the sea. And the others, the horizontal streets, contain an unending succession of hotels, restaurants, hair salons. It’s striking how many hair salons there are, and how few trees. Navia decided to book a single room for both of us on the main drag. He’s uneasy at not having cancelled the concert. The rain sweeps away any hope of a walk. But with an annoyed Navia in the room, there’s no space for anything else but to go out. I lie. I say I’m going downstairs for a smoke. From the doorway of the hotel, the rain looks less intense. So, taking an umbrella from the reception desk, I decide to get lost in the city. And getting lost in the city inevitably means choosing one of the vertical streets. The first thing I notice is the strength of the wind, of the way it feels like water. I walk down a cobbled street, hearing the whine of seagulls. And it doesn’t take me long to realize how useless it was to have brought an umbrella. The wind whirls and pulls it from my hand. It guts the wire structure that holds the fabric, drags it along and leaves it trapped in the tires of a car. Finally, I give in and carry on walking. Because there’s nothing else I can do. I shove my hands into my coat pockets and begin to discover, through the mist, the shape of that strange sea. I perceive its texture, its nuances: the grey against an amorphous, foggy background. If, for example, I had to make it into music, I would play it like that: grey against an amorphous, foggy background. My father always used to say, by way of advice, that life is a staircase. The hardest secret to master is knowing when and how to put your foot onto the next step and, if possible, for it to be the one above you and not below. That’s why he chose money over music. All the values he picked apart to explain his reasons were just excuses: I have a family, I’ve got responsibilities, you think you can just live for free. He chose money because he liked it, too, and because he was scared of music, I’m sure of it; it’s almost always a difficult road that leads nowhere. He started working at a large company when he was twenty. He had a good salary and room for growth. He rose up through the hierarchy. And, more and more, he took on a central role. His first trip abroad was in 1962. He went to New York to meet with some investors who focused on agricultural machinery production. What made the biggest impact on him during that trip was not the city or its skyscrapers, or the huge deal he ended up closing with a percentage that allowed him to buy several properties: what had the biggest impact on him, and forever, was a music. He chose money because he liked it and because he was scared of music; it’s almost always a difficult road that leads nowhere. My father couldn’t remember what the name of the New York airport was before it was called JFK. It was an unimportant detail, but for the story, for the way my father always told it, it did matter. When his plane landed and then made the necessary manoeuvres to park at the correct gate, before disembarking, the entire crew and the passengers had to wait in their seats, for safety reasons, for almost an hour so that President Kennedy’s official plane could land at the same airport that, nearly a year later, would bear his name. Those are the curious facts of history, my father would say, you never know what pieces you’re playing with or which of all those pieces you’re carrying around with you is the key, the one that will find its match and fit, bringing about what no one could imagine would happen: an event. But mine, he said, my event wasn’t having been so close to President Kennedy. Mine began to unfold, because of President Kennedy, in the taxi I took leaving the airport. I told the driver I was very late and that he should take the fastest possible route to drop me off at the hotel. The man barely nodded. And off he went. It took me a while to really notice him: he seemed to have come loose from the landscape, balanced within his own body. He had Indian features. It also took me a while to really notice the sound coming from the radio. It had the power of a moving sea, sometimes calm and sometimes overtaken by a contained violence, as if the pianist were playing in desperation. It was just the piano. But in each sound, my father said, it founded the complexity of a world. He was about to ask the driver who it was when the radio announcer began to talk over the music to say we just heard a fragment of “Poughkeepsie.” And when he heard that, my father would say, the Indian said: Oh, “Poughkeepsie!” And he kept me from hearing the full name of the musician. I asked again, before getting out of the taxi, who the musician was. But the Indian just repeated: Oh, “Poughkeepsie!” I retained just three words from all that confusion, my father would say: Poughkeepsie, Bill, and Hudson. With those three words, he started his search. On that first trip, my father scoured over twenty record stores in New York. It was the only thing he did when he wasn’t in meetings. Indeed, he felt he had come to know the city as he carried out his search, as he went from one record store to the next.
